# 113 · A nested Billing record on PlaceOrder carries @NotBlank constraints that no @Valid leads into

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: 2 new problems** | functional | medium | feature, behaviour change intended | [`OrderController$PlaceOrder`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-service/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/api/OrderController.java) | [B12: Boundary contracts](../../lib/README.md) |

> Orders gain billing details for the receipt: a nested `Billing` record with `@NotBlank` and `@Email` on its fields, added to `PlaceOrder` as a `@NotNull` component. The handler validates the request with `@Valid`, so the author expects a blank name or a bad email to be refused. Bean Validation does not step into a nested object unless the property itself carries `@Valid`, so the only check that runs on the billing details is that they are present; every test posts valid ones and passes. The module's boundary contract lists each wire type with its constraints, and the regenerated contract has a `!` line under the new property saying that the constraints on `Billing` are not checked.

Tags: [spring-boot](../README.md#tag-spring-boot), [validation-gap](../README.md#tag-validation-gap), [contract-diff-review](../README.md#tag-contract-diff-review)

## The change

Collect the customer's billing name and email with the order, for the receipt. A nested `Billing` record is added to `OrderController` with `@NotBlank String name` and `@NotBlank @Email String email`, and `PlaceOrder` gains a `@NotNull Billing billing` component. The handler already takes the request as `@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrder`. The order service does not use the details yet; that is the next change.

**Before** ([`OrderController.java`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-service/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/api/OrderController.java), line 1):

```java
package net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.ticketing.api;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import java.net.URI;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
    // ...
@RequestMapping("/orders")
class OrderController {

    record PlaceOrder(@NotBlank String holdId, @NotBlank String paymentToken) {}

    record Order(
            String id,
```

**After:**

```java
package net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.ticketing.api;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Email;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull;
import java.net.URI;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
    // ...
@RequestMapping("/orders")
class OrderController {

    /** The billing details go on the receipt; the payment itself is by the token. */
    record Billing(@NotBlank String name, @NotBlank @Email String email) {}

    record PlaceOrder(@NotBlank String holdId, @NotBlank String paymentToken, @NotNull Billing billing) {}

    record Order(
            String id,
```

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`:ticketing-service:test`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

`@Valid` on the handler parameter validates `PlaceOrder`'s own properties: `holdId`, `paymentToken` and now that `billing` is not null. Cascading into `billing` needs a `@Valid` on the component (or on the type argument, for a list); without it the validator never looks at `Billing`, and `{"name": "", "email": "not an address"}` is accepted. The constraints compile, the handler is annotated, the request type is annotated, and every test that posts an order sends a valid billing block, so nothing fails. The same shape covers a list of items (`List<Item>` where `Item` carries constraints) and a record extracted from a flat request during a refactor, which moves the constraints one level down and out of reach.

## Why the verdict is right

The wire block of the boundary contract lists each property of a request type with its constraints (`holdId: @NotBlank String`), as before. Under a property whose type carries constraints that no `@Valid` on the property or inside its type leads into, the contract has a `!` line. The change is intended, so the runner regenerates the contract and the reviewer reads the diff: a new `Billing` block with its two constrained properties, and under `PlaceOrder` the new line `billing: @NotNull Billing` followed by `! constraints on Billing are not checked: no @Valid on billing`. A new `!` line in the regenerated contract is the violation.

## What to do

Write `@NotNull @Valid Billing billing`. The regenerated contract then shows `billing: @NotNull @Valid Billing` with no `!` line, which is the diff a reviewer approves. For a list, `List<@Valid Item>` or `@Valid List<Item>` both cascade, and the contract writes the type-use form into the type (`items: List<@Valid Item>`).

## Notes

- The first example of the validation checks on a boundary contract (`lib/src/validation.rs`): a nested type's constraints with no `@Valid` leading into them (this example), a `@RequestBody` taken without `@Valid` or `@Validated` while its type carries constraints, a `@Valid` or `@Validated(G.class)` that leaves out the constraints of other groups, a constraint on a type its validator cannot handle (`@Size` on an `int`, which Hibernate Validator rejects at the first validation with `UnexpectedTypeException`), a null check on a primitive, and constraints on a non-public method of a `@Validated` bean. Each is a `!` line under the property or the handler; the library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring/fixtures/spring/Booking.java`) have one of each.
- The contract now writes the constraints inside a type, read from the class file's type annotations (`RuntimeVisibleTypeAnnotations`): `rows: @NotEmpty List<@Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z]") String>` in the ticketing service's `CreateConcert`, which earlier contracts showed as `List<String>`. The type-use constraints are where `List<@Valid Item>` cascades from, so a cascade check needs them.
- The patch changes the Java of the module, so the runner compiles it with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`. The Spring Boot tests of the module need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

**Provenance:** Constructed from a validation gap that Spring Boot developers hit when a flat request grows a nested object: Bean Validation cascades only through @Valid, the handler's own @Valid looks one level deep, and tests that send valid data cannot tell.

## Reproduce

```bash
python3 examples/tools/build.py 113
```

This applies `change.patch` to a temporary copy of the repo, runs the verifier on it, and rewrites this page.
